match.reason: None of the bank points teaches Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander societies in 1788: they cover Second World War service, post-1945 rights campaigns, health views and cultural burning, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander societies in 1788
card: In 1788 the continent and its islands were home to hundreds of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander nations. Each nation had its own Country, the land and waters it belonged to and cared for.
The nations spoke many different languages. Estimates are of several hundred languages, and many had dialects as well.
Each nation had its own laws. These covered things such as family ties, who could use which land, and how disputes were settled.

People cared for Country through practices such as seasonal movement, managing plants and animals, and passing knowledge on through stories and ceremony. Torres Strait Islander peoples lived on islands and also relied on the sea and on gardening.
draft.remember: In 1788 there were many nations, each with its own languages, laws and care for Country.

a.q: Which statement best describes Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in 1788?
opts: Many nations, each with its own languages and laws
One nation sharing a single language and set of laws
Scattered families with no shared laws or land ties
A few large groups led by one central government
a.why: The continent and islands held hundreds of nations, and each had its own languages, laws and Country. Describing one nation with one language is tempting, but it ignores this variety.
a.clue: Think about how many nations there were, and whether they were all the same.

b.q: A teacher says that in 1788 the Gunditjmara, the Noongar and the Meriam each lived under their own laws and cared for their own Country. What does this show?
opts: Societies were many and varied, each with its own laws
Only some groups had laws, and the others had none
Laws were set by one body and shared by all nations
Care for Country was the same across every nation
b.why: Each nation named has its own laws and its own Country, which shows many distinct societies. The idea of one shared law is tempting, but the card says each nation had its own laws.
b.clue: Look at the words each and its own.

a.best: Many nations, each with its own languages and laws

b.best: Societies were many and varied, each with its own laws

b.q: A student learns that in 1788 the Gunditjmara of western Victoria and the Meriam of the eastern Torres Strait differed in law, speech and how they cared for Country. What does this show?
opts: There were many separate nations, not one single people
One of the two groups had laws and the other had none
Nations far apart differed, but neighbours were alike
Only island peoples had their own Country to care for
b.why: Every nation had its own Country, languages and laws, so these two differences point to many separate nations. The idea that only distant nations differed is tempting, but neighbouring nations also each had their own laws and Country.
b.clue: Think about what every nation had, not just these two.
